Once Ravi shared the list of affected customers, they could answer directly, and the response time dropped from about 6 hours to under 1 hour.

turns.speaker: Speaker 4
turns.text: Is there something we could build so that support can look up payment events themselves next time? On mobile we had a similar problem with subscription renewals last year.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: There's an internal admin tool that shows payments for a customer, but it doesn't show the raw webhook events, which is what you'd need to spot a duplicate. Adding that view is not a lot of work, but it's not something I'd squeeze in before the idempotency fix.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Agreed. The fix comes first. Let's capture the support tooling gap in the postmortem as a follow -up rather than commit to it today. What about the public side? How did the status page work during the incident?

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: Not well. Honestly. The status page was updated 25 minutes after the first alert, and only because someone in support asked whether we were going to say anything. By then customers had been seeing errors for a long time.

turns.speaker: Speaker 6
turns.text: Which connects to the on -call problem again. Ravi was the only person who could have updated it, and he was busy actually fixing the problem.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: We'll come back to that under process, because I think the answer is the same for both. What about the numbers on the business side? Do we know what the incident cost us?

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Finance gave me a rough estimate yesterday. The failed transactions during the outage were worth about $38 ,000. Some of those customers came back and paid later the same day. So the real loss is probably closer to $15 ,000. The refunds for the duplicate charges were about $4 ,200. But that money was never really ours anyway.

turns.speaker: Speaker 4
turns.text: And we probably lost some trust, which doesn't show up in that number.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Exactly. That's the part I care about most. Payments are the one place where customers have no patience for mistakes. And they're right not to. Okay. I think that's a fair picture. Let's move on to cloud costs. Because finance has started asking questions there as well. Leo. How bad is the cloud bill this month?

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: It's not good. Our total cloud spend last month was $61 ,000. Up from about $48 ,000 three months ago. The biggest single jump is observability. Our Datadog bill alone is now $14 ,000 a month. And it was around $10 ,000 at the start of the quarter.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: What's driving the Datadog growth? We haven't added that many services.

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: Logs. Almost entirely. When I broke it down, debug level logs are about 60 % of our total log volume. Most of them come from three services. And a lot of it is the payment service logging every single Kafka message it processes. Nobody reads those logs unless something has gone wrong. And when something goes wrong we usually need the last hour. Not the last 30 days.

turns.speaker: Speaker 6
turns.text: Can't we just turn debug logging off in production?

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: We could. But then during an incident like last week's. We'd have nothing to look at. Ravi actually used those debug logs to find the duplicate charges. So I don't want to throw them away. I want to stop paying premium prices to keep them hot.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: What are the options, concretely?

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: The cleanest option is to keep debug logs in Datadog for only three days. And archive everything older than that to cold storage in our own cloud account. Cold storage is about 2 % of the cost per gigabyte. If we ever need older logs, we can rehydrate a specific time window. Which takes maybe an hour. I've tested it on one service and it works.

turns.speaker: Speaker 4
turns.text: Would that affect the mobile crash logs? We sometimes look back a couple of weeks when a crash is rare. No.

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: Crash reports go to Sentry. Not Datadog. This is only server -side debug logs. Info and error level logs would stay exactly as they are.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Three days is enough for most incidents. Last week we only needed the previous two hours.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Leo. What would the cold tier option save us per month? Roughly?

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: Roughly $6 ,000 a month. So close to half of the Datadog bill. The one -time setup is small. A few hours of configuration.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Then I don't see a reason to wait. We're moving debug logs older than three days to the cold storage tier. That's decided. Separately. I'll talk to finance about the Datadog contract myself. Because I think our committed spend level is wrong. And they're the ones who negotiated it.

turns.speaker: Speaker 6
turns.text: Should we be worried about other things growing the same way without anyone noticing? This only came up because finance asked.

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: That's exactly my concern. Right now we have no alerting on spend at all. We find out at the end of the month when the invoice arrives. I'll set up budget alerts in Terraform. So that each team gets a notification when its projected monthly spend goes more than 20 % over its budget. Then the next surprise reaches us in days instead of weeks.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Will the alerts be per service or per team? Per service would be very noisy.

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: Per team. With a breakdown by service in the alert itself. So you can see which service caused it without having 20 separate alerts.

turns.speaker: Speaker 4
turns.text: That sounds useful. Can mobile be included, even though our costs are tiny compared to the backend?

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: Sure. Every team gets one. It's the same configuration either way.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Good. What else is in the build that we should know about?

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: The other big item is the Kubernetes clusters. We run three staging clusters, and as far as I can tell only one of them is used regularly. The other two were created for projects that finished months ago, and they cost about $4 ,000 a month between them. The problem is that I'm not completely sure nobody depends on them. There might be some forgotten test environment or a demo somebody uses once a quarter.

turns.speaker: Speaker 6
turns.text: So we can't just delete them?

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: Not without checking first. Someone needs to audit the unused staging clusters and confirm with each team that nothing important is running there before we shut them down.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: I'd guess at least one of them still has the old load testing setup, but I'm not sure anyone uses it.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Let's make sure that gets done properly rather than quickly. I don't want to delete something on a Friday and find out on Monday that a customer demo depended on it.

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: Agreed. One more thought. And this is really just an idea, not a proposal. Maybe someday we could look into self -hosting Grafana for our dashboards instead of paying for the hosted version. It's not urgent and I haven't done any analysis. So please don't treat it as a plan.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Note it as an idea. If the numbers ever look compelling, bring it back with an analysis. Okay, let's move on to backups, which is a short one but important.

turns.speaker: Speaker 6
turns.text: Is this about the restore test that was supposed to happen last quarter?

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Exactly that. We take nightly backups of the main PostgreSQL database, and we've never actually tested how long a full restore takes. If we lost the primary database tomorrow, I genuinely don't know whether we'd be back in one hour or one day. That's not acceptable for a payments company. Leo, can you check how long a full backup restore actually takes?

turns.speaker: Speaker 6
turns.text: Actually, I can take that one. Leo has more than enough on his plate with the cost work, and I've been meaning to learn the backup tooling properly anyway. I'll run a full restore test on Thursday, into an isolated environment, and I'll report how long each step takes.

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: Thanks. I appreciate that. The runbook is a bit out of date, so ping me if any of the steps don't make sense. The backup bucket permissions changed in the summer.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: If you are restoring into an isolated environment, make sure the restored database can't send any emails or webhooks. We had a scare once where a restored copy started emailing real customers.

turns.speaker: Speaker 6
turns.text: Good to know. I'll disable all outbound traffic from the restore environment before starting.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Thank you, both. I'd like the restore time written down somewhere permanent once we have it, because the next question will be what our recovery time objective should be, and we can't answer that without a real number.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: From the security side, please make sure the restore environment has torn down afterwards. Restored copies of production data lying around are one of the most common findings in audits.

turns.speaker: Speaker 6
turns.text: Understood. I'll delete it the same day.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Let's turn to hiring and process. Grace, how is the hiring pipeline looking for the back -end roles?

turns.speaker: Speaker 6
turns.text: Better than last month. We have two open back -end positions. Recruiting has passed us 11 candidates in total, and after the initial screens, five of them look strong enough for the technical interview. Two of those five have competing offers, so timing matters. If we wait three or four weeks, we'll probably lose them. Um?

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Who's doing the technical interviews? Last round, the same three people did all of them, and it took a lot of time out of the sprint.

turns.speaker: Speaker 6
turns.text: That's part of what I wanted to raise. I'd like to spread the interviews across more people this time, so nobody does more than two in a week. We have six people who've been trained on the interview format, and that's enough if we plan ahead.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Agreed. Let's spread the load. Grace, can you schedule the interviews for the two back -end roles before the end of the month?

turns.speaker: Speaker 6
turns.text: Yes, I'll schedule them. I'll start with the two candidates who have competing offers, and I'll send everyone the rotation so you can see your slots in advance.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: While we're on hiring, could we hire a contractor to help with the backlog in the meantime? Even three months of help would make a big difference, especially with the idempotency work and the post -mortem follow -ups landing on the back -end team.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: No, I'm afraid not. We don't have budget for a contractor this quarter. And honestly, onboarding someone for three months would cost us almost as much time as it saves. Let's focus on the permanent hires and get them in as quickly as we can.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Understood. It was worth asking.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: It was. Now, process. Grace raised the on -call experience earlier, and I want to come back to it. Ravi was on his own for the first 20 minutes of a serious payments outage. That's not a failure on his part. It's a failure of how we set up on -call.

turns.speaker: Speaker 6
turns.text: Right. The way it works today, the primary on -call engineer is the only person paged. There's an escalation policy in pager duty, but it only escalates after 30 minutes without an acknowledgement. Ravi acknowledged quickly, so it never escalated, and he had nobody to think out loud with.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: To be honest, the hardest part wasn't the technical problem. It was trying to debug, update the status page, and answer questions in the incident channel all at the same time.

turns.speaker: Speaker 4
turns.text: On the mobile side we've been talking about the same thing. Our rotation is smaller, so it's even worse for us.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Then let's fix it for everyone. From now on, every on -call shift gets a named secondary engineer, who is paged automatically for any high severity incident, and whose job is communication. So the primary can focus on fixing the problem. That's decided, and it applies to both the back -end and mobile rotations.

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: Does the secondary need to be from the same team?

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Ideally, yes, but for the first month let's be flexible and see how it works in practice.

turns.speaker: Speaker 6
turns.text: There's a related problem. The on -call handbook is still a Google Doc, and half the team can't find it when they need it. During the incident, Ravi spent a few minutes just looking for the link to the payment provider's status page. I can move the on -call handbook into Confluence, next to the runbooks, and clean up the out -of -date sections while I'm at it.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Do that.

turns.speaker: Speaker 6
turns.text: Will do. I'll also add a short checklist at the top for the first 10 minutes of an incident.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: If you're adding a checklist, could you include a line about when to involve security? For anything touching payments or customer data, we'd like to know early rather than read about it in the postmortem.

turns.speaker: Speaker 6
turns.text: Of course. I'll add that.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Good. Before we finish, a quick look at the Partner API. Since it's affected by the Okta decision, Ravi, how does the switch to Okta change the Partner API timeline?

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: It probably helps. The original plan had 6 weeks for our own token service, and Omar's estimate for the Okta integration is 1 to 2 weeks. So even if the integration takes longer than expected, we should still be ahead of the original schedule. The rest of the Partner API, the endpoints themselves and the rate limiting, is unchanged.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: I'm happy to pair with whoever does the gateway configuration. It goes much faster when someone has done it before, and I've done it for 2 other teams.

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: How are we doing rate limiting for partners? Per Partner, or per token?

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Per Partner. Each Partner gets a quota based on their contract tier, and the gateway enforces it. Partners can have several tokens, but they all count against the same quota, otherwise someone could just create more tokens to get around the limit.

turns.speaker: Speaker 4
turns.text: Will partners be able to see their own usage? Our support team will get a lot of questions otherwise.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: Not in the first version. It's on the list, but the first version only returns the remaining quota in the response headers. A proper usage dashboard comes later.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: That's fine for the first version, as long as support knows what to tell partners. I'd like to check in on the Partner API properly next week, once the Okta integration has started and we know more.

turns.speaker: Speaker 5
turns.text: One more thing on the Partner API. Do we expect much traffic from it in the first month? It affects how I size the gateway.

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.text: The first two partners are small. Maybe a few hundred requests per minute at peak, which is nothing compared to checkout traffic. The current gateway can handle that without any changes.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Good. I think that covers everything on the agenda. To summarize the big picture, it's been a rough couple of weeks, but we now have a concrete fix for the duplicate charges, a much simpler authentication plan, a safer release date, a plan to get the cloud bill under control, and some real improvements to how we handle on -call. Thank you all, and thank you especially for joining us today. It was very helpful.

turns.speaker: Speaker 2
turns.text: Thanks for having me. I'll keep an eye out for the Okta questions.

turns.speaker: Speaker 1
turns.text: Same time next week, everyone. Thanks.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Good morning everyone, let's get started. We have a packed agenda today, so I want to keep us moving.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: First, the payments incident from last Tuesday, then a security review, the mobile release, our cloud costs, backups, and finally hiring and process.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Before we begin, we have a guest from another team joining us today.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: Hi everyone, I'm Omar. I lead application security, and I've been asked to sit in because a couple of today's topics touch authentication and the release schedule.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: Thanks for having me.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Welcome, glad you could make it. We'll get to the security items right after the incident review, so you won't have to wait long.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Okay, the payments incident. I've read the summary in the channel, but I want the whole team to hear the timeline from the person who was on call.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Ravi, can you walk us through what happened from the beginning?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Sure. So the first alert fired at 9.42 in the morning. Checkout requests started timing out,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: and within about 5 minutes the error rate on the payment service was above 30%.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: I acknowledged the page at 9.45 and started looking at the dashboards.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: The first thing I noticed was that the Kafka consumer lag on the payments topic was climbing very fast.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: It went from basically 0 to about 200,000 messages in under 10 minutes.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: Was that the consumers being slow, or was the producer suddenly sending a lot more traffic?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Both. Actually. And that's what made it confusing. Traffic was higher than normal because of the

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: marketing campaign that went out that morning. Roughly 3 times our usual peak. But the consumers

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: were also slower than they should have been. Because each payment event triggers a call to the fraud check

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: service. And that service was itself degraded. So we had more messages coming in and each one taking

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: longer to process. And how long were we actually down?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: I've seen a few different numbers floating

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: around. The full outage, meaning checkout was failing for most users, lasted 47 minutes. We had

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: partial degradation for another 20 minutes after that while the backlog drained. In total about 1,200

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: transactions failed outright. And those customers saw an error page.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: And the duplicate charges? I saw a few support tickets about people being charged twice.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Yes. That's the part I'm most worried about. When the consumers finally caught up. Some of the retried

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: messages were processed twice. The payment webhook from our provider retries if it doesn't get a

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: response within 10 seconds. And during the incident we were often slower than that. So the

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: same payment confirmation arrived 2 or 3 times. And we didn't have any protection against processing it

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: more than once. We found 86 customers who were charged twice. Support has refunded all of them

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: already.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: That's not great. Do we know why there was no dead application? I thought we had something for

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: that.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: We had dead application in the old monolith. When the payment service was split out last year,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: that logic didn't come along with it. Nobody noticed because under normal load the webhook never retries.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: It only showed up under exactly this kind of slowdown.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Okay. So what's the fix? I want to separate the

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: immediate fix from the longer term work. The immediate fix is to add idempotency keys to the

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: payment webhook handler. Every event from the provider already carries a unique event identifier.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: We store that identifier when we first process the event. And if we see it again we return success

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: without processing it a second time. It's a small change. Maybe a couple of hundred lines including

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: tests. But it completely removes the duplicate charge problem.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Where would you store the keys?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: If it's in Redis with an expiry, we need to think about what happens if Redis evicts them under memory

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: pressure. Which is exactly the situation we were in during the incident.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Good point. I'd put them in

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: PostgreSQL. In the same transaction that records the payment. That way the key and the payment are

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: written together or not at all. And there's no eviction to worry about. The table will grow. But we

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: can clean up keys older than 30 days with a nightly job.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: Does the mobile app need to change at all for

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: this?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: No. This is entirely on the server side. The app never talks to the webhook.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Alright. I don't think we need to debate this further. We're adding idempotency keys to the

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: payment webhook. Stored in PostgreSQL with the payment record. That's decided. Longer term. I'd like

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: us to look at the fraud check dependency. But not today.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: Can I ask one thing from the security side?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: Wait. When you store the event identifiers, make sure you're validating the webhook signature before

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: you store anything. Otherwise someone could replay old events or flood the table with fake identifiers.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Yes. We already validate the signature before anything else happens. And the key check would

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: come after that. I'll write the idempotency patch myself. And I should have it in review by Wednesday.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 7
speaker_transcript.text: Perfect.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: That's all I wanted to confirm.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Good. Ravi, can you also write up the full incident postmortem by Friday,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: so we can share it with the wider engineering group?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Yes. I'll have the postmortem in confluence by Friday. I'll include the timeline,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: the duplicate charge analysis, and the list of follow-up items.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: One request for the postmortem. Could we include what the on-call experience was like?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: Ravi was alone for the first 20 minutes and I think that's worth discussing separately.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Agreed. That's a fair point. And it connects to something we'll talk about at the end under

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: process. Let's move on to the security review. Over to you, since you're our guest.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: Thanks. I have two things. The first is authentication for the new partner API.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: The current plan, as I understand it, is for the platform team to build our own token service,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: issuing and validating OAuth tokens ourselves. I want to push back on that fairly strongly.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: Token services look simple and they are not. Key rotation, revocation, clock skew, refresh token

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: theft. There's a long list of things that go wrong, and every one of them becomes our problem forever.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: What's the alternative? We looked at buying something last year and the pricing was painful.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: The company already has an enterprise contract with Okta for employee login. I checked with

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: procurement yesterday, and adding customer-facing machine-to-machine tokens to that contract is

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: included up to 50,000 monthly active clients. We're nowhere near that. So the marginal cost for us is

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: effectively zero. How much work is the integration compared to building our own? I'd guess our own

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: service was going to be about six weeks. For the partner API,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: the integration is mostly

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: configuration plus validating tokens in the gateway. I'd estimate one to two weeks, and most of that

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: is testing. I'm convinced.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: Honestly, I never liked the idea of us owning cryptography code.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Does anyone want to argue for building our own? Now is the time.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Not me. I only cared about the cost, and that's answered.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Then let's make it official. We are not going to build our own token service. We'll use

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Okta for the partner API tokens instead. That's decided.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: Great. The second item is token lifetime and rotation. Right now the internal service tokens

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: never expire, which is the finding I'm most worried about from the last audit. I'd like us to rotate

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: OAuth tokens every 90 days at the very least, and ideally have the rotation automated so nobody has to

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: remember to do it. 90 days is fine for us. The services already reload credentials on restart,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: and we restart more often than that anyway.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: The mobile app doesn't use those internal tokens at

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: all, right? Just checking it doesn't affect the release.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: Correct. These are only service -to -service

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: tokens. The app uses user sessions, which are separate.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Then that's decided too. We'll rotate

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: OAuth tokens every 90 days. Automated. Is there anything else from the security side?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: One last thing. We finished the penetration test on the new checkout flow last week.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: The report isn't final yet, but there is one medium severity finding in how the app handles

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: expired sessions. I'll send the penetration test report by Thursday, with the details and a

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: recommended fix.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Thank you. That brings us neatly to the mobile release, because if there's a

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: finding in checkout, I want to understand whether it blocks the release. Hannah, where does that leave

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: the release?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: So, the current plan was to ship version 4 .2 on the 20th. The build is on test

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: flight and about 200 internal testers have been using it for a week. The feedback has been good

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: overall. The main new feature, saved payment methods, is working well, and the crash rate in

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: Sentry is at 0.8%, which is higher than I'd like but not alarming.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: The session finding isn't exactly the same payment methods flow, unfortunately. If a session expires

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: while the user is on the payment screen, the app keeps showing the same current details for a few

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: seconds before it redirects to lock in. It's not a data leak to another user, but it's not the

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: behavior we want either. That's fixable. It's a matter of checking the session state before rendering

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: the screen rather than after. But it needs a new build, another round of testing, and then app store

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: review, which has been taking three to four days lately.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: So realistically, can we still make the

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: 20th?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: Honestly, no, not safely. If the fix goes in this week, testing takes us to the middle of next

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: week, and with review time we'd be cutting it very close. I'd rather not ship a payments feature in a

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: rush right after a payments incident.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: I agree with that. The last thing we need is a second payments

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: problem in the same month.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Okay, let's move the release. We're delaying the mobile release to the

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: 27th. That gives us a week of buffer. Hannah, does the 27th work for you and the team?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: Yes, the 27th

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: works. I'll fix the session check myself, and I'll also fix the login crash this week, since that's the

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: biggest single source of crashes in Sentry right now. Out of curiosity,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: what is the login crash?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: It's an old one. On some older Android phones, if the user rotates the screen while the login request

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: is in flight, the app tries to update a view that no longer exists. It's about 40% of all our crashes,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: so fixing it should bring the crash rate down to something like 0.5%.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: While we're talking about the app, I've been wondering whether we should rewrite the mobile

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: app in Flutter. Right now we maintain two separate code bases, one for iOS and one for Android,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: and every feature costs us twice.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: I've thought about it too, and it's tempting,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: but a rewrite is at least two quarters of work for the whole mobile team,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: and we'd be shipping almost nothing new during that time.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Let's park that one. It's a real conversation, but not this quarter, and definitely not in the

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: same month as a delayed release. If someone wants to write up the trade-offs properly,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: we can revisit it at planning.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: That's fair. I just wanted it on the radar.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: It is now. Hannah, could you get the release notes ready by next Monday,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: so marketing has time to prepare the announcement?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: Sure, I'll get those done. I'll make sure they mention the saved payment methods and the crash

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: fixes.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Thank you. Before we get to costs, I want to spend a few minutes on customer impact,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: because the incident wasn't only an engineering event, our support team had a very long week,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: and I'd like everyone to understand what that looked like from their side.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: I spoke with the support led on Monday. They received just over 900 tickets in the three days

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: after the incident, compared with about 250 in a normal three-day period. Most were customers

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: asking whether their payment went through, and the most stressful ones were the duplicate charges,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: because those customers were understandably angry.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Did support have what they needed to answer the duplicate charge questions?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: I remember they were asking us for transaction lists during the incident itself.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: That was the main complaint. For the first day, they had no way to check whether a specific customer

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: had been charged twice, so every one of those tickets was escalated to engineering.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: Once Ravi shared the list of affected customers, they could answer directly,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: and the response time dropped from about 6 hours to under 1 hour.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: Is there something we could build so that support can look up payment events themselves next time?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: On mobile we had a similar problem with subscription renewals last year.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: There's an internal admin tool that shows payments for a customer,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: but it doesn't show the raw webhook events, which is what you'd need to spot a duplicate.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Adding that view is not a lot of work,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: but it's not something I'd squeeze in before the idempotency fix.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Agreed. The fix comes first.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Let's capture the support tooling gap in the postmortem as a follow-up rather than commit to it today.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: What about the public side?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: How did the status page work during the incident?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Not well. Honestly.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: The status page was updated 25 minutes after the first alert,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: and only because someone in support asked whether we were going to say anything.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: By then customers had been seeing errors for a long time.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: Which connects to the on-call problem again.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: Ravi was the only person who could have updated it,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: and he was busy actually fixing the problem.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: We'll come back to that under process,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: because I think the answer is the same for both.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: What about the numbers on the business side?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Do we know what the incident cost us?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Finance gave me a rough estimate yesterday.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: The failed transactions during the outage were worth about $38,000.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Some of those customers came back and paid later the same day.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: So the real loss is probably closer to $15,000.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: The refunds for the duplicate charges were about $4,200.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: But that money was never really ours anyway.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: And we probably lost some trust, which doesn't show up in that number.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Exactly. That's the part I care about most.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Payments are the one place where customers have no patience for mistakes.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: And they're right not to.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Okay. I think that's a fair picture.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Let's move on to cloud costs.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Because finance has started asking questions there as well.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Leo. How bad is the cloud bill this month?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: It's not good.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Our total cloud spend last month was $61,000.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Up from about $48,000 three months ago.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: The biggest single jump is observability.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Our Datadog bill alone is now $14,000 a month.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: And it was around $10,000 at the start of the quarter.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: What's driving the Datadog growth?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: We haven't added that many services.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Logs. Almost entirely.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: When I broke it down, debug level logs are about 60% of our total log volume.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Most of them come from three services.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: And a lot of it is the payment service logging every single Kafka message it processes.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Nobody reads those logs unless something has gone wrong.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: And when something goes wrong we usually need the last hour.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Not the last 30 days.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: Can't we just turn debug logging off in production?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: We could.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: But then during an incident like last week's.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: We'd have nothing to look at.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Ravi actually used those debug logs to find the duplicate charges.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: So I don't want to throw them away.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: I want to stop paying premium prices to keep them hot.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: What are the options, concretely?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: The cleanest option is to keep debug logs in Datadog for only three days.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: And archive everything older than that to cold storage in our own cloud account.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Cold storage is about 2% of the cost per gigabyte.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: If we ever need older logs, we can rehydrate a specific time window.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Which takes maybe an hour.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: I've tested it on one service and it works.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: Would that affect the mobile crash logs?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: We sometimes look back a couple of weeks when a crash is rare.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: No.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Crash reports go to Sentry.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Not Datadog.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: This is only server-side debug logs.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Info and error level logs would stay exactly as they are.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Three days is enough for most incidents.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Last week we only needed the previous two hours.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Leo.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: What would the cold tier option save us per month?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Roughly?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Roughly $6,000 a month.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: So close to half of the Datadog bill.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: The one-time setup is small.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: A few hours of configuration.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Then I don't see a reason to wait.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: We're moving debug logs older than three days to the cold storage tier.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: That's decided.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Separately.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: I'll talk to finance about the Datadog contract myself.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Because I think our committed spend level is wrong.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: And they're the ones who negotiated it.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: Should we be worried about other things growing the same way without anyone noticing?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: This only came up because finance asked.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: That's exactly my concern.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Right now we have no alerting on spend at all.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: We find out at the end of the month when the invoice arrives.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: I'll set up budget alerts in Terraform.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: So that each team gets a notification when its projected monthly spend goes more than 20% over its budget.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Then the next surprise reaches us in days instead of weeks.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Will the alerts be per service or per team?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Per service would be very noisy.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Per team.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: With a breakdown by service in the alert itself.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: So you can see which service caused it without having 20 separate alerts.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: That sounds useful.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: Can mobile be included, even though our costs are tiny compared to the backend?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Sure.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Every team gets one.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: It's the same configuration either way.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Good.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: What else is in the build that we should know about?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: The other big item is the Kubernetes clusters.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: We run three staging clusters, and as far as I can tell only one of them is used regularly.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: The other two were created for projects that finished months ago, and they cost about $4,000 a month between them.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: The problem is that I'm not completely sure nobody depends on them.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: There might be some forgotten test environment or a demo somebody uses once a quarter.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: So we can't just delete them?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Not without checking first.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Someone needs to audit the unused staging clusters and confirm with each team that nothing important is running there before we shut them down.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: I'd guess at least one of them still has the old load testing setup, but I'm not sure anyone uses it.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Let's make sure that gets done properly rather than quickly.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: I don't want to delete something on a Friday and find out on Monday that a customer demo depended on it.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Agreed.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: One more thought.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: And this is really just an idea, not a proposal.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Maybe someday we could look into self-hosting Grafana for our dashboards instead of paying for the hosted version.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 6
speaker_transcript.name: Grace
speaker_transcript.text: I'll add that.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

speaker_transcript.text: Ravi,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

speaker_transcript.name: Ravi

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: Per Partner,

speaker_transcript.text: or per token?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Per Partner.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Each Partner gets a quota based on their contract tier,

speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: and the gateway enforces it.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Partners can have several tokens,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: but they all count against the same quota,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: otherwise someone could just create more tokens to get around the limit.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: Will partners be able to see their own usage?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 4
speaker_transcript.name: Hannah
speaker_transcript.text: Our support team will get a lot of questions otherwise.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Not in the first version.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: It's on the list,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: A proper usage dashboard comes later.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: That's fine for the first version,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: as long as support knows what to tell partners.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: I'd like to check in on the Partner API properly next week,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: once the Okta integration has started and we know more.

speaker_transcript.text: One more thing on the Partner API.

speaker_transcript.text: Do we expect much traffic from it in the first month?

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 5
speaker_transcript.text: It affects how I size the gateway.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: The first two partners are small.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: Maybe a few hundred requests per minute at peak,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 3
speaker_transcript.name: Ravi
speaker_transcript.text: The current gateway can handle that without any changes.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Good.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: I think that covers everything on the agenda.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: To summarize the big picture,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: it's been a rough couple of weeks,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: but we now have a concrete fix for the duplicate charges,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: a much simpler authentication plan,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: a safer release date,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: a plan to get the cloud bill under control,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: and some real improvements to how we handle on-call.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Thank you all,

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: and thank you especially for joining us today.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: It was very helpful.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: Thanks for having me.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 2
speaker_transcript.name: Omar
speaker_transcript.text: I'll keep an eye out for the Okta questions.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Same time next week, everyone.

speaker_transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
speaker_transcript.text: Thanks.
